qt: to the Commission Friedrich Pürner (NI) Subject:

The Commission has announced that it will submit an anti-corruption strategy to protect the Union’s financial interests by the end of 20261. At the same time, the Union is granting Ukraine a EUR-90-billion loan, of which over 28 billion is earmarked with defence without any preconditions to undertake reforms. The funds continue to flow into a country which is having significant trouble stemming corruption. In May 2026 for instance, the Ukrainian National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) brought money-laundering charges against the former head of the Presidential Office2. In August 2026, it further uncovered an alleged criminal network said to include members of parliament and officials from the Presidential Office3. Rather that engaging in any reforms, the relevant committee of the Ukrainian parliament subsequently recommended leaving several anti-corruption bills off the agenda4. In its answer to written question P-000015/20265, the Commission stated that Ukraine should set up a separate account, and that monitoring requirements would be included in the relevant agreement. 1.
What binding oversight and claw-back conditions apply to the loan, including the defence funds?
Does the Commission also intend to make disbursements from the defence component contingent upon progress in the fight against corruption, in particular adoption of the postponed legislation?
Will the planned anti-corruption strategy also apply to EU funding for third countries and candidate countries, and if not, why not?
